nameStory: The Two-ridged Ramshorn gets its name from the distinctive pair of ridges that spiral around its coiled shell, resembling a ram's curled horn. The 'ramshorn' part comes from this classic spiral shape that's shared by all snails in this family, while 'two-ridged' sets this species apart from its smoother relatives.
description: The Two-ridged Ramshorn is a small freshwater snail that breathes air despite living underwater. Its shell coils in a flat spiral like a tiny cinnamon roll, typically reaching about half an inch across. Unlike many aquatic snails, this species comes to the surface regularly to breathe air through a simple lung. You'll find these snails gliding along underwater surfaces or occasionally floating at the water's surface.

idTips.label: Two spiral ridges
idTips.description: Feel for two distinct raised ridges that spiral around the shell's coils - they're prominent enough to catch your fingernail when you run it gently across the surface

idTips.label: Flat coil shape
idTips.description: The shell lies nearly flat like a coiled rope rather than forming a tall spire - it's wider than it is tall

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: The shell feels relatively smooth between the ridges and has a slightly glossy appearance when wet

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Adult shells typically measure about 0.4 to 0.6 inches across - roughly the size of a large pea when fully grown

idTips.label: Surface breathing
idTips.description: Watch for the snail coming to the water's surface to breathe - you might see a small silvery air bubble trapped against its body

habitat: Look for Two-ridged Ramshorns in quiet freshwater environments like ponds, slow streams, and marshy areas throughout New England. They prefer waters with plenty of aquatic vegetation and organic debris on the bottom. You'll often find them in shallow areas near shore where they can easily reach the surface to breathe.

seasonality.spring: Active snails emerge as waters warm, often found grazing on early aquatic vegetation and algae films on submerged surfaces.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when snails are most visible, frequently coming to the surface to breathe and easiest to spot on warm, calm days.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to slow down, often found deeper in the water column as surface temperatures cool.
seasonality.winter: Become dormant in bottom sediments, though shells may still be found washed up on shores or in dried pond margins.

funFact: Despite living underwater, Two-ridged Ramshorns actually drown if they can't reach the surface to breathe air - they're essentially aquatic snails with lungs instead of gills, making them more like tiny underwater mammals than fish!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other ramshorn snails, but the two prominent spiral ridges are the giveaway - run your finger gently around the shell and count the ridges. Remember 'TWO ridges for TWO-ridged Ramshorn.'
contextualKnowledge: The name 'ramshorn' can be confusing because these snails are completely unrelated to rams - it's purely about the shell shape resembling a curled horn. Some people also call them 'wheel snails' because of their flat, circular appearance.
compareHints: Since this is the only Helisoma species commonly found in New England, compare it to other ramshorn snails in the Planorbidae family. Other ramshorns typically have smoother shells or different ridge patterns - the Two-ridged Ramshorn's pair of prominent spiral ridges makes it distinctive. The ridges are much more pronounced than the subtle growth lines you might see on other ramshorn species.
